findings.claim: The productive asset base is heavy-manufacturing capacity for turbines, transformers and switchgear — genuinely scarce industrial plant that takes years to add.
findings.label: ANALYST ESTIMATE

findings.claim: Capacity is the binding constraint and it is being relieved on a published schedule: 20 GW of annual gas turbine output in Q3 2026, 24 GW in 2028, and actions in train to reach 30 GW in 2030.
findings.label: MANAGEMENT GUIDANCE

findings.claim: Against a 116 GW gas turbine backlog and 20 GW of annual output, the queue is roughly 5.8 years long at current capacity, falling to under 4 years once 30 GW is reached.
findings.label: ANALYST ESTIMATE
findings.unit: years of backlog at current output

findings.claim: That arithmetic is the whole cyclical question. A 5.8-year queue supports scarcity pricing; a sub-4-year queue with three suppliers expanding does not, and the backlog is a fixed quantity that depletes as it is delivered.
findings.label: ANALYST ESTIMATE

findings.claim: Electrification faces a genuinely tighter and longer-lived bottleneck than gas turbines: transformers and switchgear have global lead times measured in years, with far more constrained supplier capacity and far less new entry.
findings.label: ANALYST ESTIMATE
findings.source: Derived from the electrification market structure; corroborated by the parallel Siemens Energy backlog in this batch

findings.claim: Prolec GE contributes approximately USD 3.1bn of the USD 14.5-15.0bn Electrification revenue guidance — a transformer business acquired into exactly the shortage the segment is monetising.
findings.label: MANAGEMENT GUIDANCE

findings.claim: Capital intensity is moderate for the scale of expansion under way, and the company has funded a 50% capacity increase while doubling the dividend and increasing the buyback authorisation — which indicates the expansion is not straining the balance sheet.

risks.text: The backlog is a depleting stock. At 30 GW of output the 116 GW queue is under four years, and three suppliers are expanding into the same demand.
Capacity expansion by all major suppliers simultaneously is the classic mechanism by which industrial shortages become gluts.

catalysts.text: 20 GW annual output run rate confirmed

conclusions: The asset base is genuinely scarce heavy-manufacturing capacity, and the bottleneck is real — but it is being relieved by the company itself on a published schedule.
The queue arithmetic is the whole cyclical question: 116 GW against 20 GW of output is 5.8 years; against 30 GW it is under four. The backlog is a depleting stock, not a perpetual annuity.

Electrification faces a tighter and longer-lived bottleneck than gas turbines — transformers and switchgear have less new entry and longer lead times — which makes it arguably the better business inside the group.
Capital intensity is manageable: the company is funding a 50% capacity increase while doubling the dividend and raising the buyback authorisation.
thesisImpact: Phase 2 reframes the backlog from an asset to a clock. The USD 176bn is real, but it converts over roughly six years at current capacity and under four at the 2030 target. Phase 5 must value what the business earns after the queue clears, not annualise the queue.
